notes:
Now Pulpit.I've written verse-by-verse notes on Song of Solomon 8 below, but some of what you asked for is missing. The tool hit its usage limit partway through, so I never reached newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org, bibleodyssey.org, the Lutheran sites, gotquestions.org or the Pentecostal sites other than Enduring Word. I found nothing on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter, so that part is left out, and I only saw part of David Guzik's Enduring Word page.

What the notes do cover:
- Enduring Word (Guzik) and Precept Austin
- The commentaries by Ellicott, Gill and Wesley, and the Pulpit Commentary
- A Spurgeon sermon
- Short excerpts on Bible Hub and StudyLight from Benson, Barnes, Matthew Henry, Adam Clarke, the Biblical Illustrator and the Preacher's Complete Homiletical Commentary
- The NET Bible notes

**Frequent sources:**
- [EW] https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-8/
- [Ellicott] https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/songs/8.htm
- [Pulpit] https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/songs/8.htm
- [Gill] https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/songs/8.htm
- [Wesley] https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/songs/8.htm
- [Precept] https://www.preceptaustin.org/song_of_solomon_commentary_8
- [NET] https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=sos+8%3A5-14

---

## Overview: how the chapter is read

There are three main approaches in the sources:
- **Human love, straightforwardly:**
  - Guzik reads the chapter as mature married love that keeps its passion as it grows more settled. [EW]
  - Ellicott reads it as a poet's memories of a real courtship and marriage. [Ellicott]
- **Human love as a picture of Christ and the Church:** The Pulpit Commentary says the Song need not be read as allegory. It is a song of human love, but that love is a symbol of something divine, so it often applies verses to Christ and the Church. [Pulpit]
- **Full allegory:**
  - Gill (Baptist) reads the whole chapter as the Church and Christ. [Gill]
  - Wesley's notes do the same, and add a story line about the Jewish church and the Gentiles. [Wesley]
  - Spurgeon preaches v. 5 devotionally as being about Christ. https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/leaning-on-our-beloved

---

## Verse by verse

**v. 1**
- **Plain reading:**
  - In Ellicott's view, the bride remembers the time before they could marry. She couldn't openly show her love then, and wished they were related so they could embrace without people talking. [Ellicott]
  - Precept Austin explains that in ancient Hebrew culture husbands and wives didn't usually show affection in public, but a brother and sister could. She says "like" a brother; she doesn't wish he really were one. [Precept]
  - The NET Bible notes call vv. 1–2 a "lover's wish song," like an ancient Egyptian love song, and say the wish is deliberately exaggerated. [Precept]
- **Pulpit Commentary:** A blood tie can't be broken the way a marriage can be broken by fickle feelings. She wants their love to be that secure. As a symbol, it is the Church longing for the closest fellowship with the Saviour. [Pulpit]
- **Gill (Baptist):** "Like a brother who nursed at my mother's breasts" points to Christ's real incarnation and his close kinship with his people. The "mother" is the heavenly Jerusalem. [Gill]
- **Wesley (Methodist):** The Church wants a closer union and communion with Christ. "Outdoors" means in the open streets. [Wesley]

**v. 2**
- **Who "taught me"?**
  - The Pulpit Commentary reports a split. Jerome and Luther take it as "*you* would instruct me," meaning Solomon teaches her. Hitzig and the Revised Version take it as her mother teaching her, as a mother teaches a young bride.
  - It quotes Delitzsch: either way the verse shows her heart. [Pulpit]
- **Spiced wine and pomegranate juice:**
  - Ellicott says these were valued Eastern drinks and points back to 1:2, 5:1 and 7:9. [Ellicott]
  - The Pulpit Commentary says there is no hidden love symbol here. It reads the gifts as the Church offering her treasures in return for the blessings she receives. [Pulpit]
- **Gill:** The "mother's house" is God's house, a school where believers learn Christ's ways. [Gill]
- **Wesley:** Her gifts and graces will all be used to serve Christ. [Wesley]
- **NET notes (via Precept Austin):** The verse is read openly as sexual. Precept Austin quotes the NET's reading that she wishes to offer her breasts to Solomon in married love, outdoors kisses in v. 1, private intimacy indoors in v. 2. [Precept]
- **Jewish reading:** The Pulpit Commentary reports that the Targum takes it as bringing "King Messiah" into the sanctuary to teach her to fear God. [Pulpit]

**v. 3**
- The NET and Precept Austin note that this repeats 2:6. Carr says a girl longing for closeness is a common theme in ancient love poetry. [Precept]
- Gill reads it as the Church enjoying Christ's presence in her mother's house. [Gill]

**v. 4**
- **Guzik (EW):** This is the third time the charge appears (2:7; 3:5). For the relationship, it means "don't let us go too fast." For passion, it means not starting until both can be fully satisfied. [EW]
- **Precept Austin:** It quotes G. Campbell Morgan: love is sacred and must not be trifled with, and toying with it destroys the ability to love. [Precept]
- **Pulpit Commentary:** It notes that "by the gazelles and does" is missing this time, and suggests natural love has been raised into a higher, companion-like love, from *eros* to *agape*. [Pulpit]
- **Gill:** He also notes the missing phrase, and says it could be read "why would you stir up…?" [Gill]

**v. 5**
- **Who speaks the opening question? The sources disagree:**
  - Benson: the daughters of Jerusalem or friends of the couple, admiring the marriage. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/songs/8-5.htm
  - Gill agrees it is the daughters of Jerusalem. [Gill]
  - Wesley: the bridegroom, asking the question so he can answer it. [Wesley]
  - The Pulpit Commentary: country people or relatives near the bride's home. [Pulpit]
  - Guzik: a relative. [EW]
- **Where are they?** Barnes says the scene has moved to the bride's birthplace. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/songs/8-5.htm
- **"Wilderness":** The Pulpit Commentary says it means open country, not barren desert. [Pulpit]
- **"I roused you under the apple tree":**
  - Ellicott: "I awoke love in you." The tree marks where they became betrothed. [Ellicott]
  - The Pulpit Commentary agrees that the change to feminine endings ("I roused *you*," meaning her) is backed by the Syriac. [Pulpit]
  - Carr (in Precept Austin) disagrees. The Hebrew endings are all masculine, so she is speaking to him, and he finds no textual support for the change. [Precept]
- **Spurgeon (Baptist), sermon "Leaning on Our Beloved":**
  - The verse links communion with Christ to growth in grace.
  - The text says she leans on the whole person of the Beloved, not just "the arm," as it is usually misquoted.
  - She leans because she is weak, the road is dangerous, the way goes uphill, and he is strong enough to carry her weight.
  - https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/leaning-on-our-beloved
  - Guzik summarizes Spurgeon's reasons. [EW]
- **Wesley:** "I raised you" means raised from being dead in sin, under Christ's shadow (compare 2:3). The "mother" is the Church. [Wesley]
- **Gill:** The mother in labour stands for the apostles and ministers, who labour until Christ is formed in people. [Gill]
- **Pulpit Commentary:** A call to remember our first love for Christ. [Pulpit]
- **Older Latin and Catholic allegory (as Ellicott reports it):**
  - The Vulgate says her mother was "corrupted" there, which Ellicott says sounds like allegory.
  - Later interpreters made the tree the Cross, the one loved there the redeemed Gentiles, and the corrupted mother the synagogue that rejected Christ.
  - Ellicott also notes the Greek (LXX) adds "made white" and the Vulgate adds "flowing with delights." [Ellicott]

**v. 6**
- **The seal:**
  - Ellicott: a symbol of something especially precious (compare Jer 22:24; Hag 2:23). [Ellicott]
  - The Pulpit Commentary: a signet worn on a cord near the heart (Gen 38:18) or on the hand. She asks never to drift out of his thoughts. [Pulpit]
  - Guzik: married love should be like a seal, permanent, belonging and secure. He quotes Kinlaw calling it a poetic "until death do us part." [EW]
  - Gill: the high priest carrying Israel's names on his heart, a picture of Christ. [Gill]
  - Wesley: engraved tablets worn on the chest, or a signet on the arm. [Wesley]
- **"Jealousy":**
  - Ellicott: strong passion, used in a good sense, as the parallel lines show. [Ellicott]
  - The NET notes quote Coppes: the KJV takes the word badly, but it can mean "ardent zeal." [NET]
  - Guzik is unsure whether a good or bad sense is meant. He quotes Spurgeon that real love for Christ will be stirred to jealousy by his enemies. [EW]
  - The Pulpit Commentary: love so intense it won't put up with a rival. [Pulpit]
- **"The fiercest blaze" (literally "flame of Yah"):**
  - Ellicott says it is the only place God's name appears in the book, and it is used to mean "supremely great." [Ellicott]
  - Guzik quotes Carr, who prefers this superlative idiom to "a flame from God." [EW]
  - Gill gives both: a superlative, or love lit by the Lord's Spirit. [Gill]
  - The Pulpit Commentary renders it "a very flame of the Lord," compares it to lightning, and calls the passage a high point of the poem. [Pulpit]
- **Other readings:**
  - Matthew Henry: the Church asks for her union with Christ to be confirmed. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/song-of-solomon/8-7.html
  - Wesley: the bride is pleading not to be left. [Wesley]
- **Catholic translation:** The Douay-Rheims has "jealousy as hard as hell, the lamps thereof are fire and flames." https://biblehub.com/catholic/songs/8-6.htm

**v. 7**
- **Ellicott:**
  - The Hebrew repeats the verb for emphasis: *he* would be utterly despised.
  - He thinks the passage reflects a real story of two hearts tested and proved true. [Ellicott]
- **NET:** Love can't be bought; it is worth more than all wealth. [NET]
- **Guzik:** He quotes Glickman: "Sex can be bought; love must be given." His four pictures of love:
  - seal: giving yourself to the other
  - death: permanence
  - fire: be careful where and with whom love is kindled
  - priceless [EW]
- **Pulpit Commentary:** It applies the "waters" to persecution of the Church. [Pulpit]
- **Allegorical readings:**
  - Gill: the Church's love can't be quenched by persecution or by flattery. [Gill]
  - Wesley: the waters are troubles or temptations. [Wesley]
- **Catholic translation:** The Douay-Rheims renders it "many waters cannot quench charity." https://biblehub.com/catholic/songs/8-6.htm

**v. 8**
- **Where vv. 8–14 belong:** Ellicott says most commentators feel the poem really ends at v. 7. Some scholars think vv. 8–14 were added later. He himself sees the closing verses as more memories of the same story. [Ellicott]
- **Plain reading:**
  - Ellicott and Guzik take it as her brothers, back in her childhood, planning for the day she would be asked in marriage. [Ellicott] [EW]
  - The Pulpit Commentary instead has the bride asking Solomon about her own younger sister. It mentions Delitzsch's view (the brothers answer) and rejects it. [Pulpit]
- **Allegorical readings:**
  - Gill: the little sister is the Gentile church, spoken of by the Jewish church. [Gill]
  - Wesley agrees: the Gentiles not yet grown. [Wesley]
  - The Pulpit Commentary lists other suggestions (Beza; Hengstenberg; "those weak in faith") and calls them endless guesses. It keeps only the broad idea of love reaching out to others. [Pulpit]
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentary/song-of-solomon/8-8.html

**v. 9**
- **Wall versus door:**
  - Ellicott: chastity versus its opposite. If she stays pure, they will provide a fine marriage for her; if not, they will guard her. He calls this one of the strongest arguments that the book's theme is chaste married love. [Ellicott]
  - The NET notes agree: reward if she is virtuous, restraint if she gives in to temptation. [NET]
  - Guzik says something similar, and adds a point about families helping shape young people's morals. [EW]
- **Pulpit Commentary's different view:**
  - It thinks "door" as a picture of seduction is far-fetched.
  - Wall and door just do different jobs, strength and beauty, and both are honoured.
  - It lists many allegorical readings (Zöckler) and says such detail turns people away from the book. [Pulpit]
- **Wesley:** Christ answers: "We" (Father, Son and Spirit) will strengthen Gentile believers. If they are weak in faith ("a door"), he will not reject them. [Wesley]
- **Jewish reading:** The Homiletical Commentary notes Rashi read it as Israel being open to seducers. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/song-of-solomon/8-8.html

**v. 10**
- **Ellicott:** She protests that she is pure and of age to marry. [Ellicott]
- **Guzik:** Guarding her honour earlier is why she now has peace in marriage. [EW]
- **Pulpit Commentary:** "Peace" (*shalom*) is probably a play on the name Solomon. It says the verse rules out the "shepherd" theory (that she loved someone else and was taken by the king). [Pulpit]
- **NET:** Her breasts are like towers in two senses: they defended her purity, and they are beautiful. [NET]
- **Wesley:** The Jewish church speaking: "by your grace I am what you want my sister to be." [Wesley]

**vv. 11–12**
- **Ellicott:**
  - "Baal-hamon" is a wordplay ("lord of a multitude"), a hidden reference to Solomon's many wives.
  - His harem is like a vineyard rented out to tenants. Her one true love is a vineyard she keeps herself.
  - The 200 shows what polygamy costs. [Ellicott]
- **NET:** Solomon's vineyard is literal, but "my vineyard" is herself. Unlike his vineyard, she isn't for sale; her love is freely given. [NET]
- **Guzik:** She knows her own worth, and freely gives herself to Solomon. He quotes an unnamed preacher who applied the 200 to keeping ministers paid and respected. [EW]
- **Pulpit Commentary:** It reads the vineyard as her wish to bear abundant fruit for the king. [Pulpit]
- **Wesley:** The vineyard is the Church, bought with Christ's blood. The 200 is the support due to ministers. [Wesley]
- **Where is Baal-hamon?** The Homiletical Commentary lists guesses: Baal-gad, Baalbek, Jerusalem, the Gentile world. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/song-of-solomon/8-8.html

**v. 13**
- **Who speaks?**
  - Ellicott: the lover, remembering how he envied the companions who could hear her. [Ellicott]
  - The Pulpit Commentary: the bridegroom asks the country bride to sing. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/song-of-solomon/8-13.html
- **Adam Clarke (Methodist):** The bridegroom asks permission to leave early in the morning. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/song-of-solomon/8-13.html
- **Wesley:** "Gardens" are the many congregations. "Let me hear it" means the Church's prayers, praise and preaching while Christ is away. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/song-of-solomon/8-13.html
- **Guzik:** He notes some read vv. 13–14 as a separation. [EW]

**v. 14**
- **Ellicott:** It echoes 2:17 and sums up the whole story of courtship and marriage. [Ellicott]
- **Guzik:** The Song ends with the same passion it began with. [EW]
- **Wesley:** "Finish your work and take me to yourself." [Wesley]
- **Homiletical Commentary:** It applies the verse to Christ's presence now and his second coming. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/song-of-solomon/8-8.html

---

## Where the traditions differ (from these sources only)

- **Allegory versus plain sense:**
  - Gill (Baptist) and Wesley (Methodist) read every verse as Christ and the Church, including the Jewish church / Gentile church story in vv. 8–10.
  - Spurgeon (Baptist) preaches v. 5 the same way.
  - Guzik (Enduring Word) and Ellicott read the chapter as human love and marriage.
  - The Pulpit Commentary takes a middle line: human love as a "type," but it criticizes detailed allegory. (Links above.)
- **Lutheran:** The only Lutheran point I found is the Pulpit Commentary's note that Luther took v. 2 as "you would instruct me."
- **Catholic and Orthodox:** I found these only second-hand: the Vulgate and allegorical readings Ellicott reports for v. 5, and the Douay-Rheims wording for vv. 6–7.
